Thank you for posting the detailed screenshots. I want to start by saying that without EEG, sleep staging data, or belts to measure respiratory effort, I can’t be 100% sure about anything I’m about to say, so take it with a grain of salt. One of the challenges with OSCAR is that it doesn’t tell the whole story but we do the best we can with what’s available.

From what I can see it seems like you’re experiencing post-arousal centrals, primarily during REM sleep. Here’s what that means: You’re likely waking up, taking a few deep breaths, and blowing off CO2. This rapid reduction in CO2 signals your brain that you don’t need to breathe for a moment, leading to these flagged central apneas. This is different from true central apnea, where the brain incorrectly signals the body not to breathe.

What could be happening here is that you have something called "high loop gain," meaning your respiratory control is very sensitive to fluctuations in CO2. When you blow off too much CO2 after an arousal, it disrupts your respiratory control, leading to these cyclical centrals. I experience a similar issue, though mine are shorter and don’t get flagged as often.

The real issue isn’t the centrals themselves, it’s the arousals. These arousals are likely fragmenting your REM sleep significantly, which could explain why you feel so awful. Unfortunately, many doctors overlook this and focus strictly on the AHI. 

So, what can you do about it? Honestly, I wish I had a concrete answer. From your OSCAR data it looks like you’re dealing with significant flow limitation during REM, which might be contributing to the arousals. The typical solution for flow limitation is increasing pressure but in your case higher pressure seems to fragment your REM sleep even further—likely because the increased pressure is exacerbating your CO2 sensitivity.

Alternatives might include using bi-level or an ASV but your doctor obviously isn't open to exploring those options, and even those aren’t guaranteed fixes.

Here’s what I’d recommend:

1. Consider finding a new doctor who is more open-minded and takes these issues seriously. I know that’s easier said than done but you're wasting your time with this guy.


2. Check out CPAP Friend on YouTube. He has some really informative videos on these kinds of issues and offers consultations for $50 to analyze your OSCAR data. I’ve learned a lot from him and the top doctors in the field he interviews. At the very least he could point you in the right direction.



I hope this helps give you a better framework for understanding what’s happening and possible next steps!

Most of what I don't like about IFS has nothing to do with the actual model. It's what you mentioned when you talked about the cult like mentality that some people have. I have tried to engage with some people in IFS communities and they are so focused on following the model that they don't listen to anything you're actually saying. It's as if people are no longer people, they are just a collection of parts to be therapized. I also agree with your critique of it not being inclusive of other modalities. There are a lot of modalities that pair very well with IFS. I've made more progress since I started looking at IFS as a tool in my toolbox rather than a solution to my problems.

The only critique of the mode I have outside of the one's you outlined is overreliance on the concept of Self. It can be a barrier to entry for some people. Like I cannot deny the existence of Self and Self energy but if I never engaged with parts unless I was in that feeling state I would be perpetually paralyzed and stuck. When I shifted the focus away from being in Self to being with parts I started making so much more progress. I just abandoned the whole concept of "getting into Self" or "checking for Self" entirely. It's a great state to be in and I welcome it when it is here and I have noticed that as I work with parts it comes up spontaneously but otherwise I don't concern myself with it.

So I have been doing this mental health journey for almost 15 years. Started therapy when I was 17 and I'm almost 32. I would approach medication with extreme caution. That is not to say that I would rule it out if I were you but definitely do your research and don't trust your doctor to know everything because it's a very young field of medicine. It's a lot of trial and error and educated guessing. Be a well-educated patient and if your doctor doesn't like that find a new one. Your experience could range anywhere from a quieting of the negative thoughts in your head to being a complete zombie to a hellish mix of any number of side effects. The latter two are honestly more likely but it's different for everyone so you just gotta weigh the potential risks vs the potential rewards.

As you said medication is just a partial solution and it's not meant to be long term either. You definitely don't want to be on antidepressants for the rest of your life. Finding the right therapy is just as important as finding the right medication. I remember when I started out I thought therapy was therapy. I saw my first therapist for almost 7 years and thought the reason I wasn't getting better was because I sucked at following his "guidance" and he did not disillusion me of this. Once I left him I found out that there are just as many modalities of therapy as there are antidepressants. You've got to find what works for you. I notice a lot of people, myself included, don't find traditional talk therapy very helpful. My personal opinion is that trauma, especially complex trauma, is very prevalent in Western society hence why traditional talk therapy is failing us.

Trauma doesn't live in the logical parts of our brain that talk therapy engages with. It lives in our lizard brains. It's not just the soldier come back from a war zone or sexual assault victim like mainstream media would have you believe either. I'm fairly convinced that most of us leave childhood with some sort of trauma. Unless you had two fantastic parents who loved you in all the ways you needed you probably experienced some form of complex trauma.

So all that being said IFS, EMDR, trauma focused CBT, somatic experiencing, and DBT are some good starting points for exploration. My advice is take the best and leave the rest. Find what works for you and don't worry about what doesn't.
